methodNote: This is NOT a first-contact evidence run and it is NOT a governance record. It is one request,
authorised by D20-A, to answer an engineering question D20 deliberately left open: what does Google
actually do when asked from this infrastructure?
D20 refused Google on the publisher's own terms without contacting them, and that refusal is
UNCHANGED by this file. `governanceStatus` was REFUSED before the request and is REFUSED after it;
`effectiveEnabled` was false before and is false after; both are asserted inside the runner so that
the run cannot silently coincide with somebody flipping them.
THE ENGINE SUCCEEDED. That is recorded here as a technical fact and it is NOT a reason to enable
Google. Inferring permission from an engine having worked is the precise inversion that
`engine-governance.ts` exists to prevent. Whether a working engine may be used is a separate
production-governance decision, and it has not been taken.
A future reader must not read this file as evidence supporting activation. It is evidence about

request.via: our own SearXNG instance, http://127.0.0.1:28888, production SearxngClient
request.subject: Bernard Madoff
request.subjectNote: A public figure chosen for the live-smoke file, deliberately reused so this result is comparable with the same day's five-engine table. Not a customer and not a screening subject.
request.categoriesNote: Never sent. SearXNG treats `engines` and `categories` as a union, so a category would have pulled in engines this run was not authorised to touch.
request.instanceReconfiguredNote: `infra/local/searxng/settings.yml` still carries `google news: disabled: true`. The request reached the engine only because it named the engine explicitly, which is the property that file's own comment already documented. Nothing was edited to permit this.

outcome.enginesCreditedNote: Asserted in the runner: the instance must not have run an engine the request did not name. It did not.

finding: This is the notable part, and it is the one that contradicts a D20 assumption rather than the
licence finding. D20 recorded a second, independent defect: a Google News RSS <item><link> is a
news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMi<token> redirect rather than the publisher's article URL, so the
feed cannot meet FR-09 provenance even with permission.
That defect is specific to the RSS feed. The SearXNG `google news` engine scrapes
google.com/search?tbm=nws instead, and every one of the ten URLs it returned was an ORIGINAL
PUBLISHER URL with no Google-hosted redirect at all. So D20's provenance objection does NOT carry
over to this route, and anyone reopening the question should not cite it as though it did.
The licence objection is untouched and remains the whole of the refusal: Google's Terms of Use
permit personal non-commercial use and forbid automated access, and scraping the news results page
is if anything further from permitted than reading the RSS feed D20 examined.

beforeRequest.reasoning: The 3600s suspension from the 10:51 CAPTCHA had expired roughly two hours before this run. Had it still been in force the instance would have short-circuited and the run would have observed its own breaker rather than Google, which is exactly the trap the twenty-fifth session's 0ms DISABLED_BY_POLICY reading fell into from the other direction.

afterRequest.recordedErrorsForEngine: 50% SearxEngineCaptchaException — unchanged absolute count, halved because this successful request is now the second sample
evidence: `docker logs erly-adverse-search-searxng-1 | grep -i google` shows exactly two entries, at
09:30:52 and 10:51:32, both predating this run. No entry was written by it.
`GET /stats/errors` moved `google news` from 100% to 50% on the same single ErrorContext, which
is what one success recorded against one historical error looks like. A new CAPTCHA would have
added a log line and held the percentage at 100.

governance.tenantImpact: None. No tenant search can reach Google: `effectiveEnabled` is computed as `integrated && tenantEnabled && governanceStatus !== 'REFUSED'`, so the REFUSED reading blocks execution whatever any tenant switch says. This diagnostic bypassed that gate deliberately and only inside its own file, which is not reachable from the request path.
governance.dataImpact: None. No lead, candidate, document, finding or database row was produced. The ten URLs above exist only in this file and in the run's console output.

openQuestionRaised: Google works from this egress and returns original publisher URLs. The refusal therefore now rests
on the licence alone, with no technical defect left standing behind it.
That makes the production-governance question a live one rather than academic, and it is NOT
answered here. D20-A explicitly does not authorise enabling Google, and this run did not. Raising
it means reopening D20 on the terms D20 quoted — the personal-non-commercial clause and the
automated-access clause — or taking the documented alternative D20 already recorded: Google's
Programmable Search Engine / Custom Search JSON API, which is contractually licensed for commercial
use and paid beyond a free allowance.
